headline: Italy Fines Meta €805 Million; Accounting Files It Under 'Hilarious Rounding Error'
subheadline: *Regulator says the company accessed photos and videos of 20 million users without specific consent; Meta reportedly located the sum between the sofa cushions.*
author: Ingrid Halvorsen, Privacy & Regrets Desk
seoTitle: Italy Fines Meta €805M for Looking at Your Photos
seoDescription: Satire: Italy fined Meta €805 million for accessing 20 million users' photos without consent. Meta's accountants filed it under 'hilarious rounding error.'
sourceEvent: Italy's Data Protection Authority has fined Meta €805 million for accessing photos and videos belonging to about 20 million smartphone users without their specific consent. The penalty is one of the largest privacy fines the Italian regulator has issued to a social media company.

social.x: Italy has fined Meta €805 million for looking at 20 million people's photos without consent. Meta's accounting department has filed the amount under 'hilarious rounding error' and asked Italy if it takes payment in exposure.
social.facebook: Italy's Data Protection Authority has fined Meta €805 million for accessing the photos and videos of around 20 million smartphone users without their specific consent — a sum insiders confirm was recovered from a petty cash drawer labelled 'Tuesday.' Meta responded that users had, in a sense, consented by owning phones. The company has offered to settle in 40 billion ad impressions, or one (1) lightly used VR headset, whichever Italy prefers.
social.linkedin: Italy's €805M penalty against Meta raises important questions about proportionate enforcement — primarily whether a fine representing roughly six hours of revenue constitutes a deterrent, a cost of doing business, or a rounding error with a flag on it. Full analysis below.

altHeadlines: Meta Vows to Appeal Italian Fine, Once It Finishes Looking Through the Evidence
Italy Fines Meta €805 Million; Meta Earns It Back Before Regulator Finishes Sentence

body:
ROME — Italy's Data Protection Authority has fined Meta €805 million for accessing the photos and videos of roughly 20 million smartphone users without their specific consent, an amount insiders confirmed was recovered from a petty cash drawer labelled 'Tuesday.'

The regulator found that the social media giant had helped itself to users' camera rolls with what officials described as 'the confidence of a man opening a fridge that is not his.' Meta disputed the characterisation, noting that the fridge door was technically ajar.

'We take privacy extremely seriously,' a Meta spokesperson said. 'We take it everywhere. It comes with us. It is, if anything, always with us. Now that we say it out loud, we see how that could be part of the problem.'

The €805 million penalty is among the largest the Italian watchdog has issued, though analysts cautioned against describing it as significant. 'Eight hundred and five million euros sounds like a lot until you remember Meta earns it back in roughly the time it takes to accept its own terms and conditions,' said one industry analyst, who asked not to be named for fear of appearing in Meta's photo library.

In Menlo Park, the fine reportedly triggered an emergency meeting of the company's senior leadership, which was adjourned after four minutes when someone located the correct amount in lost-and-found.

Affected users responded with resignation. 'Honestly, it's a relief,' said local man Benedetto Farro, 44, whose camera roll consists of 6,000 photos of receipts, a pigeon, and his own ear taken by accident. 'For years nobody was looking at these. It's nice that someone was finally getting some use out of them.'

Meta confirmed it intends to appeal, arguing that users did consent — broadly, spiritually, and in paragraph 40,000 of a document formatted to be read by no one. The company stressed that the photos were accessed 'respectfully' and were each assigned a small party hat in the metadata.

In response to the ruling, Meta has overhauled its consent flow. Users will now be asked 'May we?' with two clearly labelled options: 'Yes' and 'Later, but also yes.' A third option, 'No,' is understood to be in beta testing and is not expected to launch in this century.

The Italian authority welcomed the fine as a landmark moment for European privacy enforcement, before reportedly receiving a notification that Meta would like to view its photo — a notification that has so far refused to go away.

At press time, Meta's accounting department had rounded the €805 million down to zero, describing the discrepancy as 'within tolerance.'
